blocks.text: “EZEKIEL THE PRIEST, THE SON OF BUZI” (EZEKIEL 1:3), MADE “A WATCHMAN UNTO THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL” · EXILE & RETURN
Ezekiel. Among the captives by the river Chebar, from the fifth year of Jehoiachin's captivity.
Jehoiachin · Zedekiah · Nebuchadnezzar · Pharaoh king of Egypt
Visions of God by the river Chebar
Called, as four accounts tell it
“the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God”

“The word of the LORD came expressly unto Ezekiel the priest … and the hand of the LORD was there upon him.” The hand of the LORD comes upon him again before the visions of the temple, the dry bones and the new temple. Ezekiel 1:3 Ezekiel 3:22 Ezekiel 8:1 Ezekiel 37:1 Ezekiel 40:1

The spirit lifted him up and carried him: to the captives at Tel-abib, “in the visions of God to Jerusalem”, and back “into Chaldea, to them of the captivity”. Ezekiel 3:12–15 Ezekiel 8:3 Ezekiel 11:24–25
From the textGod calls him “son of man” throughout the book: the words “son of man” stand in 94 verses of the King James text of Ezekiel. Ezekiel 2:1 Ezekiel 37:3

He was told to shut himself in his house and that his tongue would cleave to the roof of his mouth, except when God opened it to speak; his mouth was opened the evening before the fugitive from Jerusalem came. Ezekiel 3:24–27 Ezekiel 24:27 Ezekiel 33:21–22

He was told to “put forth a riddle, and speak a parable”, and to take up lamentations for the princes of Israel, for Tyrus and for Pharaoh; he complained, “they say of me, Doth he not speak parables?” Ezekiel 17:2 Ezekiel 19:1 Ezekiel 20:49 Ezekiel 27:2 Ezekiel 32:2

The elders sat before him in his house to enquire; the people came to hear “as a very lovely song”, but “they hear thy words, but they do them not.” Ezekiel 8:1 Ezekiel 14:1 Ezekiel 20:1–3 Ezekiel 33:30–32

From the textThirteen passages are dated by the years of Jehoiachin's captivity, most of them to the month and day. Ezekiel 1:1–2 Ezekiel 8:1 Ezekiel 20:1 Ezekiel 24:1 Ezekiel 26:1 Ezekiel 29:1 +7 more
Scholars' viewDriver (1891) dates the call to 592 BC and the latest date in the book (29:17) to 570 BC; Keil (1876) reckons the same two dates as 595 and 572 BC. Ezekiel 1:2 Ezekiel 29:17 [2][19]
“Behold, I am against thee, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers”
The word in its main themes
The glory leaves the temple, and returns
“the glory of the LORD came into the house by the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east”
“I the LORD have spoken it: it shall come to pass, and I will do it; I will not go back”
“Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.”
They shall know that I am the LORD
A new heart and a new spirit
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you”
“I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away”
To whom the word was spoken
“Are ye come to enquire of me? As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I will not be enquired of by you.”
“And thou, profane wicked prince of Israel, whose day is come, when iniquity shall have an end”
“Son of man, set thy face against the Ammonites, and prophesy against them”
“Because that Edom hath dealt against the house of Judah by taking vengeance”
“Behold, I am against thee, O Tyrus, and will cause many nations to come up against thee”
“Because thine heart is lifted up, and thou hast said, I am a God”
“Behold, I am against thee, O Zidon; and I will be glorified in the midst of thee”
“Behold, I am against thee, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers”
“Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?”
“Ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the LORD”
“Behold, I am against thee, O Gog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal”
The siege drawn on a tile
Smiting the hands, stamping the foot
The new temple and the river
1 The call by the Chebar Ezekiel 1:1–3:27
6 The watchman and the news Ezekiel 33:1–33
7 Shepherd, new heart, dry bones, Gog Ezekiel 34:1–39:29
8 The new temple and land Ezekiel 40:1–48:35
WHERE THE NEW TESTAMENT QUOTES IT · 12
Each band joins a chapter of Ezekiel to the New Testament books quoting it (3 books).
Who stood with him, and against him
The elders of Judah and of Israel
The man with the measuring reed
The one who escaped from Jerusalem

From the textThe latest date in the book is “the seven and twentieth year, in the first month, in the first day of the month”; the vision of the new temple is dated the twenty-fifth year. Scripture does not tell how Ezekiel's life ended. Ezekiel 29:17 Ezekiel 40:1

Benjamin of Tudela describes “the Synagogue of Ezekiel” by the Euphrates with “the sepulchre of Ezekiel” behind it, said to have been built by King Jeconiah and his people after Evil-merodach released him, with a lamp kept burning day and night over it.[29] Who says so: Benjamin of Tudela, Itinerary (tr. Adler 1907), 1165–1173

The Jewish Encyclopedia says the traditional burial place “is shown at Kefil near Birs Nimrud”, and that the mausoleum dates “probably from the time of the califs”.[31] Who says so: Jewish Encyclopedia, "Ezekiel's Tomb", 1903
From the finding of the law in Josiah's eighteenth year
The Targum and Jerome, as reported by C. F. Keil (1876); Ideler

Keil reports this reading of “the Chaldee paraphrast and Jerome”, and objects that “no trace … can elsewhere be pointed out of the existence of a chronology dating from these events”. Ezekiel 1:1–2 [19]
From the reign of Nabopolassar of Babylon
“Many of the older expositors”, as reported by C. F. Keil (1876)
Keil notes that Nabopolassar became king of Babylon in the year this would point to, but that “nothing … is know of any such era”.[19]
Hengstenberg, as reported by C. F. Keil (1876); E. G. Hirsch and K. H. Cornill in the Jewish Encyclopedia (1903)

Keil rejects it because the added month and day point “to an era generally recognised”. The Jewish Encyclopedia holds that if the date be understood “to apply to the age of the prophet … this view still has the appearance of probability”.[19][30]
C. F. Keil (1876); S. R. Driver (1891)
Keil says the era “is matter of dispute, and can no longer be ascertained with certainty”; Driver says the epoch “is uncertain”.[19][2]

Ezekiel does not say how old he was, or from what “the thirtieth year” (Ezek 1:1) is counted.
Ezekiel 4 does not say from when the 390 and 40 years of iniquity are reckoned.
Ezekiel never names Zedekiah, the Pharaoh of chapters 29–32, or the prince of Tyrus.
The text does not itself connect “yet shall he not see it” (Ezek 12:13) with the blinding of Zedekiah in 2 Kings 25:7; the reader is left to compare them.
The New Testament does not name Ezekiel.
Scripture does not say how, when or where Ezekiel died.
